newsitem.title: CHINA: China B shares seen up but party congress looms.
newsitem.headline: China B shares seen up but party congress looms.

text.p: China's hard-currency B shares were poised to rise further over the next month, but a major Chinese Communist Party congress in September or October would overhang the market, analysts and brokers said on Sunday.
Both Shanghai and Shenzhen B shares soared on Thursday and Friday on the long-awaited return of foreign and Hong Kong funds to the market.
Shanghai's B share index closed up 8.92 percent to 87.676 points on Friday, while Shenzhen gained 4.96 percent to 158.73 points.

China "plays" in Hong Kong, including H shares -- shares of Chinese enterprises listed in Hong Kong -- have surged in recent days, and foreign investors have now turned to the relatively inexpensive B shares, which are reserved for foreign investors, analysts said.
"B shares have lagged so much they still have more room to go up before the party congress," said an analyst at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai.
The 15th party congress, the first such gathering since the death of leader Deng Xiaoping, is expected to chart the future of China's development, analysts said.
An announcement on Friday that Beijing would place control of its two stock exchanges with the central government removed a negative rumour from the market and should support futher rises, they said.
"It's better to get news like this out of the way," said a broker at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai. "The market will probably go up on this."

The announcement was viewed as the last in a series of crackdown moves since May to rein in soaring markets, including the sacking of the head of China's market watchdog and stiff punishment of brokerages and listed firms for speculation.
But analysts stopped short of predicting a new bull run for the B-share markets with the upcoming party congress looming on the horizon and other possible short-term hiccups.
"Recent rises were largely speculative," said an analyst at Sun Hung Kai Investment Services in Shenzhen. "I'm pessimistic about interim results and expect they could hit the markets quite hard."

B share interim results for 1997 have proved to be a mixed bag so far with many firms yet to report before the end-August deadline. Companies with poor results typically wait until shortly before the deadline.
Expectations have been building that the party congress would see the announcement of a bail-out for state firms, which would also help many listed companies, analysts said.
Direction for the market for the rest of 1997 would hinge on the outcome of the meeting, they said.

"People are expecting something out of the party congress and if nothing negative comes out, then we would at least cruise sideways for the rest of the year," said the foreign securities firm analyst.
But expectations for the congress have been built up so much that investors could sell purely out of disappointment if clear policies for state firms were not forthcoming, analysts said.
"Much of the recent gains seem grounded on speculation, and I think the congress will sober people up," said an analyst at J&A Securities in Shenzhen.
If the party congress was read as positive. the Shanghai B share index was likely to test 100 points and the Shenzhen B index 170 points before the year was out, analysts said.
